links.note: The Council of Chalcedon deposed Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, in October 451, after he refused three summonses to answer his accusers. prose_changes.old: After Chalcedon, the Christians of Syria and Mesopotamia who refused the council's formula were in a harder position than their Egyptian counterparts: inside the Roman Empire, without a patriarchal throne of their own, and for long stretches under Justinian without legal standing at all. Their leader Severus of Antioch was driven from his see in 518 and wrote from exile in Egypt for twenty years. Their communities kept meeting, and their clergy kept being ordained, largely because of Jacob Baradaeus. A bishop consecrated under the protection of the Ghassanid Arab kings and of the empress Theodora, who spent decades traveling in disguise across Syria and Mesopotamia ordaining priests and bishops for a church the empire would not recognize. John of Ephesus, himself a Miaphysite bishop and one of Justinian's own missionaries, wrote down fifty-eight portraits of these people while it was happening. When the Byzantine defeat at Yarmouk in 636 ended the empire's power to enforce against them, what emerged was a separate hierarchy that had never stopped functioning.
prose_changes.new: After Chalcedon, the Christians of Syria and Mesopotamia who refused the council's formula lived, like the Egyptian Miaphysites, inside the Roman Empire. But they lost the throne of Antioch, and for long stretches under Justinian they had no legal standing at all. Their leader Severus of Antioch was driven from his see in 518. He withdrew to Egypt, as many of his bishops did, and went on writing from exile. Their communities kept meeting, and their clergy kept being ordained, largely because of Jacob Baradaeus. He was made a bishop at the request of the Ghassanid Arab king Harith, with the backing of the empress Theodora. For decades he traveled across Syria and Mesopotamia, ordaining priests and bishops for a church the empire would not recognize. He would finish his work in a district in a day and a night, then move thirty or forty miles on. The bishops hunting him never caught him. John of Ephesus, himself a Miaphysite bishop and one of Justinian's own missionaries, wrote down fifty-eight portraits of these people while it was happening. In 636 the Byzantine defeat at Yarmouk ended the empire's power to enforce against them. What emerged was a separate hierarchy that had never stopped functioning.
prose_changes.reason: Three fixes. (1) 'Harder than their Egyptian counterparts: inside the Roman Empire' set up a contrast that fails, since Egypt was also inside the empire and Alexandria too passed to a Chalcedonian (Evagrius IV.11, line 8202, Zoilus). Now stated as what is shown: Antioch lost in 518 (Evagrius IV.4, 7894-7898). (2) 'Twenty years in Egypt': the vendored texts show the withdrawal to Alexandria (Ps.-Zachariah VIII.5, 10222-10224) and a stay in Constantinople in 535-536 (IX.19), not twenty years there; narrowed. (3) 'In disguise' is not in John of Ephesus; he says Jacob outran his pursuers (Lives 50, 26330-26337), and the nickname Burd'ana means 'the man of the patchwork garment' (editor, 26246). The sentence fragment 'A bishop consecrated ...' is made whole.

prose_changes.old: This communion had no legal right to exist under Justinian, so its bishop Jacob Baradaeus spent decades traveling in disguise across Syria and Mesopotamia, secretly ordaining priests and bishops under the protection of Ghassanid Arab kings and the empress Theodora. When Byzantine power collapsed at Yarmouk in 636, what emerged was a hierarchy that had never stopped functioning despite having no legal standing at all.
prose_changes.new: This communion had no legal right to exist under Justinian. Its bishop Jacob Baradaeus was consecrated at the request of the Ghassanid Arab king Harith, with the empress Theodora's backing. He spent decades crossing Syria and Mesopotamia, ordaining priests and bishops one step ahead of the bishops hunting him. When Byzantine power collapsed at Yarmouk in 636, a hierarchy emerged that had never stopped functioning, despite having no legal standing at all.
prose_changes.reason: 'In disguise' and 'secretly' are not in John of Ephesus (Lives 50, 26330-26337: he outran his pursuers). 'Under the protection of' narrowed to what Lives 50 shows: Harith asked, Theodora ordered the consecrations (26702-26704; 31198-31206). Long sentences split.

prose_changes.old: This church is a direct heir of the Syriac Christian tradition, and the St Thomas Christians of India belonged to its communion.
prose_changes.new: This church is a direct heir of the Syriac Christian tradition. By the 550s a bishop appointed from Persia served at Kalyan in western India. A traveler also found a church on the pepper coast further south.
prose_changes.reason: 'The St Thomas Christians of India belonged to its communion' is more than the one vendored witness for this period shows. Cosmas, Christian Topography III (cosmas-indicopleustes_christian-topography_mccrindle1897.txt 7209-7211), names a church in Male and a Persian-appointed bishop at Calliana; McCrindle identifies them as Malabar and Kalyan (7222, 18802). Matches the Inferential-Thin link.

prose_changes.old: In 424 the bishops of the Persian Empire declared that their catholicos at Seleucia-Ctesiphon answered to no bishop beyond their own frontier — a church living under a Zoroastrian shah, deliberately independent of the Roman world and its councils. It gave a different answer to the question of Christ than either Chalcedon or the Miaphysites, following the tradition of Theodore of Mopsuestia in holding firmly to the distinctness of his divinity and his humanity, and its opponents fixed the name "Nestorian" on it. Its intellectual center was the School of Nisibis, which had written statutes governing the students' day, their lodging and their discipline. Formation documents of a kind almost nothing else this early has left. Its communion stretched far beyond Mesopotamia: the St Thomas Christians of India belonged to it. When the Sasanian empire fell to Arab armies by 651, the church carried straight on under new rulers and kept expanding eastward.
prose_changes.new: In 424 the bishops of the Persian Empire declared that their catholicos at Seleucia-Ctesiphon answered to no bishop beyond their own frontier. This was a church living under a Zoroastrian shah. It had accepted the Nicene creed in 410, but it would answer to no Roman bishop. It gave a different answer to the question of Christ than either Chalcedon or the Miaphysites. Following the tradition of Theodore of Mopsuestia, it held firmly to the distinctness of his divinity and his humanity. Its opponents fixed the name "Nestorian" on it. Its intellectual center was the School of Nisibis, which had written statutes governing the students' day, their lodging and their discipline. These are formation documents of a kind almost nothing else this early has left. Its communion stretched far beyond Mesopotamia. In the 550s a traveler named Cosmas found a bishop appointed from Persia at Kalyan, in western India. He also found a church on the pepper coast further south. When the Sasanian empire fell to Arab armies by 651, the church carried straight on under new rulers and kept expanding eastward.

Now says that. (2) The St Thomas sentence narrowed to Cosmas (as in prose change 3). The fragment 'Formation documents of a kind ...' is made a sentence, and the long Theodore sentence is split; no fact changed.

prose_changes.old: The same institution continued unbroken into the Byzantine centuries that followed, and is the direct ancestor of the Eastern Orthodox churches today. The pattern set here — emperor and patriarch as two authorities within one Christian commonwealth — became the model Byzantium exported to the Balkans and to Russia. Hagia Sophia stood as the largest church in the world for nearly a thousand years and changed what a church building could be. Justinian's legislation fed into Orthodox canon law, and the hymns of Romanos are still sung. Its harder legacy is the divisions its pressure helped harden: the separations of 451 were still unhealed when the empire lost Egypt and Syria altogether.

The Russian half is narrowed to what Mouravieff (1842) shows: bishops first came from Constantinople and Yaroslav had the Nomocanon translated (mouravieff_history-of-the-church-of-russia_blackmore1842.txt 1426-1431), and Kyiv's St Sophia was named after the church where Vladimir's envoys believed (1463-1467). prose_changes.old: In the ravines between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea, and in the villages around Gaza, monastic settlement multiplied in the century after Chalcedon into something like a second population — laurae where hermits lived apart through the week and gathered on Sundays, and communal houses holding hundreds. What makes this Christian tradition unusually visible is that its own paperwork survives: Cyril of Scythopolis's carefully dated lives of Euthymius, Sabas and their successors, and roughly 850 letters from two recluses near Gaza, Barsanuphius and John, answering monks, married couples, sick people and local officials one question at a time. These were firm supporters of Chalcedon, and they were pulled hard into the empire's doctrinal fights, including the purge of Origenist teaching in the 550s that split their own houses. The Persian army's sack of Jerusalem in 614 tore through the desert monasteries, and the survivors wrote down what had been lost.
prose_changes.new: In the century after Chalcedon, monks settled in the ravines between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea, and in the villages around Gaza. They grew into something like a second population. There were laurae, where hermits lived apart through the week and gathered on Sundays, and communal houses holding hundreds. What makes this tradition unusually visible is that its own paperwork survives. Cyril of Scythopolis wrote carefully dated lives of Euthymius, Sabas and their successors. Two recluses near Gaza, Barsanuphius and John, left roughly 850 letters answering monks, married couples, sick people and local officials one question at a time. Most of the Judean houses came to support Chalcedon. When Euthymius accepted the council, his biographer says, nearly all the desert monks would have followed. A rival monk named Theodosius turned many of them against it. Near Gaza, Peter the Iberian became bishop for the council's opponents. The monks were pulled hard into the empire's doctrinal fights, including the purge of Origenist teaching in the 550s that split their own houses. The Persian army's sack of Jerusalem in 614 tore through the desert monasteries, and the survivors wrote down what had been lost.
prose_changes.reason: 'Firm supporters of Chalcedon' is true of Euthymius's and Sabas's line but not of the whole movement this entry covers, which includes Gaza. Cyril of Scythopolis, Life of Euthymius (Cotelier, cyril-scythopolis_vita-euthymii 36066-36072), says almost all the monks would have followed Euthymius had Theodosius not drawn them off; Ps.-Zachariah III.4 (2670-2675) has Peter the Iberian made bishop for Gaza by that Theodosius. The Origenist split is supported (Evagrius IV.38, 9503-9507, the New Laura). The two long opening sentences are split; no fact changed.

prose_changes.old: A great deal of what Eastern Orthodox monasticism still does comes from here. The liturgical order associated with Sabas's monastery underlies Orthodox worship to this day. The Ladder of Divine Ascent, written at Sinai just after this period, is still read aloud in Orthodox monasteries every Lent; and Dorotheus of Gaza remains standard spiritual reading. Two of the houses standing in this window — Mar Saba in the Judean desert and Saint Catherine's at Sinai — are still inhabited, among the oldest continuously occupied Christian communities anywhere.
prose_changes.new: Much of what Eastern Orthodox monasticism still does draws on these houses. A book of services named after Sabas, the Typikon of Saint Sabas, was printed at Venice from 1515. Parts of it entered the Orthodox service books. The Ladder of Divine Ascent was written at Sinai just after this period. It is still read aloud in Orthodox monasteries every Lent, and Dorotheus of Gaza remains standard spiritual reading. Two of the houses standing in this window are still inhabited: Mar Saba in the Judean desert and Saint Catherine's at Sinai. They are among the oldest continuously occupied Christian communities anywhere.

The three present-day claims (Lenten reading, Dorotheus, the two monasteries) are kept and flagged to Mark: no vendored text can speak to present practice.
